content: In materials science, coercivity, also known as the coercive field, refers to the strength of the external magnetic field required to reduce the magnetization of a ferromagnetic material to zero after it has been magnetized to saturation. Coercivity is typically measured in units such as oersted or ampere per meter and is denoted as ( H_C ). A ferromagnetic material with a high coercive field is classified as a hard or permanent magnet, which is commonly used in applications like hard drives, floppy disks, magnetic tapes, and magnetic separation. Conversely, a material with a low coercive field is considered soft and is often utilized in microwave devices, magnetic shielding, transformers, or recording heads. Coercivity can be measured using a ( B-H ) analyzer. To experimentally determine the coercivity of a magnetic material, the hysteresis loop or magnetization curve is measured. This is typically done using instruments such as a vibrating-sample magnetometer or an alternating-gradient magnetometer. The coercivity corresponds to the point on the magnetization curve where the applied magnetic field causes the magnetization to cross zero. If an antiferromagnetic solid is present in the sample, the coercivities measured during increasing and decreasing magnetic fields may differ due to the exchange bias effect. The coercivity of a material also depends on the time scale over which the magnetization curve is measured. Over long time scales, the magnetization of a material subjected to a reversed field slightly smaller than the coercivity may gradually decay to zero. This phenomenon, known as magnetic creep, occurs when the reversal of magnetization via domain wall motion is thermally activated and influenced by magnetic viscosity. At high frequencies, the increasing coercivity poses a significant challenge to achieving higher data rates in high-bandwidth magnetic recording, further complicated by the need for higher coercivity in media with increased storage density. At the coercive field, the vector component of the magnetization along the direction of the applied field becomes zero. Magnetization reversal occurs through two primary mechanisms: rotation and domain wall motion. When magnetization reverses by rotation, the magnetization component along the applied field is zero because the vector points in a direction orthogonal to the applied field. In contrast, when magnetization reverses via domain wall motion, the net magnetization is minimal in all vector directions because the moments of individual domains cancel each other out. Magnetization curves dominated by rotation and magnetocrystalline anisotropy are typically observed in relatively perfect magnetic materials used in fundamental research. However, domain wall motion is a more significant reversal mechanism in real engineering materials, as defects such as grain boundaries and impurities act as nucleation sites for reversed-magnetization domains. The role of domain walls in determining coercivity is complex, as defects can both pin domain walls and nucleate them. The dynamics of domain walls in ferromagnets are analogous to the behavior of grain boundaries and plasticity in metallurgy, as both involve planar defects. As with any hysteretic process, the area enclosed within the magnetization curve during one cycle represents the work performed on the magnet. Common dissipative processes in magnetic materials include magnetostriction and domain wall motion. Coercivity serves as a measure of the degree of magnetic hysteresis and, therefore, characterizes the energy losses in soft magnetic materials for their typical applications. For hard magnets, figures of merit include squareness (( M(H=0)/M_s )) and coercivity, although the energy product (saturation magnetization multiplied by coercivity) is most commonly cited. The 1980s saw the development of rare-earth boride magnets with high energy products but undesirably low Curie temperatures. Since the 1990s, new exchange-spring hard magnets with high coercivities have been developed.
